history.content: Is bulk migration better than vMotion?

Bulk migration can migrate multiple VMs concurrently, provide more consistent bandwidth use, allow for scheduling during a maintenance window, and accommodate VMs using different virtual CPU features. However, individual VMs migrate more slowly, there is brief downtime during the migration, and VMs that depend on disk ordering and UUIDs (like Oracle RAC) can have issues. vMotion, in opposition, migrates a single VM very quickly, allows the VM to remain live during the process, and supports shared disk clusters with the multi-writer flag enabled. However, it can generate fluctuations in bandwidth use, may not support certain types of disk configurations, and requires the network to meet certain performance criteria .I you need to migrate many VMs at once, maintain consistent network usage, or accommodate different virtual CPU features, bulk migration might be better. But if you need to minimize downtime, migrate a single VM quickly, or use shared disk clusters with the multi-writer flag enabled, vMotion might be a better choice. A vMotion migration is initiated from the remote ESXi proxy host to the destination vSphere physical ESXi host, while it receives data from the source CGW across the tunnel. When vMotion is employed, unlike the bulk migration option, only a single VM migration operation runs at a time. As a result, for many VMs to be migrated, it is recommended to use vMotion only when downtime is not an option or if a risk in rebooting the VM exists. However, like standard vMotion, the VM can be live during the process.
